Recipe for
high-grossing
movies

Box-office success is hard to compare across decades: a 2001 release lives in a different market than a 2024 release. This project first builds a fair, year-aware measure of success, then tests 3,781 US theatrical films across four lenses (attributes, network, plots, reviews) to find the patterns that hold up under both definitions of success.

The Question

What characteristics define high-success US films?

We measure success in two complementary ways and run every analysis under both, so any reported pattern has to survive both definitions. Toggle the switch top-right at any time. The four lenses below organise the rest of the site.

  • 01Attributes · What role do budget, runtime, rating and popularity play?
  • 02Network · Which collaborations of cast & directors recur among successful films?
  • 03Plots · Do successful films share plot language?
  • 04Reviews · What review & reception patterns track success?

About the dataset

3,781 US theatrical films released between 2000 and 2026. The data combines two sources we built ourselves: a TMDb extraction (revenue, budget, cast, directors, votes, audience reviews) with an inflation-corrected profit column in 2026 dollars, joined on tmdb_id with Wikipedia plot summaries and critical-reception sections. The full pipeline is documented in §2 of the explainer notebook.

b · Provenance

How it was assembled

Two extraction pipelines and one inflation pass, all reproducible from the notebook. Re-running is gated behind RUN_API_EXTRACTION = False; the cached CSVs in the repo are loaded by default.

Source · TMDb. Revenue, budget, runtime, vote counts, audience reviews, top-cast, directors, genres, production companies. Extracted in §2.1 via the /movie/{id} endpoint with credits,reviews,release_dates appended, 100-thread concurrent batches, 100-req/s rate-limit safety.
Source · Wikipedia. Plot summaries and critical-reception sections retrieved via the MediaWiki API in §2.2. Title resolution by search + page-parse; section text isolated by regex on level-2 headings. Global rate-limit lock to stay under 150 req/min, checkpointed every 200 rows.
Inflation adjustment. CPI from FRED series CPIAUCSL. box_office_surplus_adj_2026 = (revenue − budget) × CPI2026 / CPIrelease_year. Methodology in §2.3.
Two success metrics ("tracks"). Track A = absolute inflation-adjusted profit. Track B = each film's rank within its release year (time-invariant). Use the toggle top-right to switch between them.

Attributes we use

The master table carries more columns than the analysis needs. The working subset, organised by which of the four lenses each column feeds, is below.

Defines both tracks: Track A reads box_office_surplus_adj_2026 directly, Track B takes its percentile rank inside each release_year. The same columns minus the headline metric are the numeric features ranked by Spearman ρ on the Attributes tab; genres drives the genre-median bars.

Lens 02 · Network
Cast & directors
top_cast(first 10)directors

The people columns from TMDb. top_cast lists the first 10 credited actors per film; directors lists all credited directors. Together they record who worked on each film and are the basis for the collaboration analysis in the Network tab.

Lens 03 · Plots
Wikipedia plot text
wiki_plot(free text)

Source for the plot-themes word-clouds and the per-community vocabulary cards on the Language tab. TF-IDF is fitted on the full 3,781-film corpus so common plot words don't dominate the per-cluster lists. Chi-squared collocations are merged into single tokens so multi-word phrases can surface.

Lens 04 · Reviews
Audience & critic reception text
reviews(TMDb · audience)wiki_critical_response(Wikipedia · critic)

Two parallel corpora for the Language tab. TF-IDF on each surfaces the vocabulary that separates the top from the bottom of the active track; VADER computes per-tier compound sentiment for the gradient bar. Terms that show up on both sides earn an overlap badge.

Kept for provenance but not modelled. overview (TMDb's short blurb, superseded by the longer Wikipedia plot), production_companies (extracted but not analysed), us_regular_theatrical (used as a row-level filter; every kept film has it true), and the identifier columns tmdb_id, title, release_date.

Methodology

Two ways of accounting for time

Before asking what successful films have in common, we have to decide what "successful" means. A 2001 dollar, a 2025 blockbuster market, and a pandemic-era release year are not directly comparable, so the analysis follows two tracks throughout. Only patterns that survive both reach the final recipe.

Track A: Whole period

metric = inflation-adjusted profit ($2026)

Every film's revenue minus budget, expressed in 2026 dollars. Absolute scale: how much money, comparable across 25 years.

Track B: Per-year relative

metric = profit percentile within release year

Each film ranked 0–100 against only the films it competed with that year. This removes the year effect entirely: pure relative success.

A single picture motivates the dual-track design. The chart below counts, for each release year, how many films enter the top 10% under three competing definitions of success. If a definition were truly fair across time, the count would sit close to a constant: roughly one in ten of that year's cohort, every year.

Top-10% films per year, under three definitions of success

x-axis = release year, y-axis = number of films in the top decile that year. Raw whole-period profit over-rewards recent films (nominal dollars grow); inflation-adjusted whole-period profit still leans toward the recent past, just less; per-year percentile is flat by construction. Click a legend entry to hide a series.

Per-year percentile is flat by design. The raw and adjusted curves are not, which is exactly the problem Track B exists to solve. The Attributes tab applies both tracks to the actual film-level features (popularity, budget, rating, runtime, genre) to see which signals survive both fairness conventions.

02 · Attributes

What the numbers actually reward

Track A · inflation-adjusted profit Track B · per-year percentile

With two fair definitions of success in hand, the first concrete question is the simplest: which film-level attributes actually correlate with each? We rank four numeric features (audience vote count, inflation-adjusted budget, critical rating and runtime) by Spearman ρ against the active track's success metric, then re-cut the data by genre and by budget tier. The three numbers below summarise how much of success these attributes capture, and where the picture changes between Track A and Track B.

Under absolute profit, raw popularity dominates and a four-feature linear model explains 59% of the variance, though this track is inflated by time and part of that fit reflects chart-topping recent franchises.Judged per-year, popularity weakens and critical rating jumps in importance. The four-feature model now explains 38%: a harder, fairer target that better separates films from their year, not from history.

59%

of success variance explained by just four numeric attributes. A high fit means these attributes are correlated with success, not that they cause it.

0.70

Spearman ρ for the top correlate, audience vote count. Popularity signals that audiences are already engaged, which amplifies revenue regardless of quality.

+.01

Spearman ρ for critical rating . Under Track A, critical rating shows a moderate positive correlation with absolute revenue — smaller than audience reach, but not negligible. Under Track B it gains weight: once films are judged within their release year, quality becomes a more reliable separator.

The chart below makes the ranking concrete. Bars extend rightward for positive Spearman correlation; switching the active track at the top of the page reshuffles the order in place. Watch vote count shrink and critical rating grow as you move from absolute dollars to per-year percentile. This is the single biggest shift on this page.

Attribute correlation with success

Spearman ρ between each numeric feature and the active success metric (Track A · inflation-adjusted profit). Range −1 (perfect inverse) to +1 (perfect agreement); zero = no monotonic relationship.

The ranking shifts when you switch tracks. Under absolute profit, audience reach dominates because blockbusters that open wide accumulate revenue regardless of when they were released. Under per-year percentile, critical rating gains ground: once a film is judged only against its own year, quality becomes a more reliable separator. Budget and runtime remain secondary under both definitions.

02 · Budget

Two strategies, one valley

Films are sorted into five equal-population budget tiers (inflation-adjusted), each holding roughly 750 titles, from cheapest (Q1) to priciest (Q5). The three panels below report the median outcome inside each tier under the active track.

Under absolute profit, the ROI curve is U-shaped: cheap films return most per dollar (low denominators flatter the ratio), mega-budgets are the safest absolute earners, and the middle bleeds. Mid-range films need a real audience but are not large enough to dominate marketing share-of-voice.

Per-year, the curve is near-monotonic: bigger budgets buy higher relative rank almost linearly. Inside a single release year, scale is the surest way to beat your cohort. The mid-budget valley flattens out once we stop comparing across decades.

02 · Genre

Genre sets the ceiling

Median success by genre, ranked under the active track. Track A reports median inflation-adjusted profit per film: animation, adventure and sci-fi lead because they're produced at scale, open wide, and lean on enduring IP.Track B reports median per-year percentile (50 = an average film for its year): the same big-tent genres still lead, but documentaries and dramas (typically modest in absolute dollars) climb the table once each film is judged against its own year's cohort. The strongest signal in both views: animation tops the ranking either way.

Genre ranking

01 · Collaboration Network

The connectors aren't the earners

Track A · Absolute profit

Node size = inflation-adjusted profit ($2026). Large nodes are franchise anchors — the biggest earners across 25 years. The most connected people are rarely the biggest earners.

Track B · Per-year percentile

Node size = average percentile rank within each film's release year. Removes franchise scale — rewards films that outperformed their competition, not just their era.

Graph topology is fixed: one node per person, one edge per pair that shared a film. Only node value changes with the dropdown. A signal that survives both tracks is a robust signal.
Node size = chosen value (bigger = more) Colour = collaboration community Edge = shared films (brighter = more) Hover to focus a cluster · drag to move · scroll to zoom · double-click to reset
Track A · Absolute adjusted profit
Franchise anchors top the value ranking. Downey Jr., Johansson, Evans lead — MCU scale dominates when raw dollars count. High degree (Seth Rogen, Jonah Hill) does not predict this: prolific ≠ profitable.
Switch node size to "Degree" to see how completely the ranking changes.
Track B · Per-year percentile
Rankings shift toward consistent outperformers. People whose typical film beats its release year rise — a harder, fairer test than raw scale. Franchise anchors still appear, but the field compresses.
A signal that survives both tracks is a robust signal.

Is this network actually structured?

A modularity of 0.73 sounds high — but high compared to what? Two null models answer this: the configuration model rewires every edge while keeping each person's exact collaborator count; Erdős–Rényi keeps only totals. Each runs 100 times.
Do successful people cluster together?
Newman attribute assortativity: are high-success people more likely to collaborate with other high-success people than chance predicts? Tested against 200 label-shuffle runs on the active track.

Who matters — by which definition?

Three lenses on influence, each picking up a different shape. Toggle the node-size dropdown above to resize the graph by each. Key finding: prolific ≠ profitable — the most connected people are rarely the most valuable.

What each cluster is about

The collaboration network groups people who repeatedly work together. Each card below identifies a cluster by its three highest-grossing signature films and its most distinctive plot vocabulary. IDF is computed across the full 3,781-film corpus (not within communities) so generic words don't dominate; chi-squared collocations from notebook §3.6.5 are merged into single tokens so multi-word phrases can surface (e.g. tony_stark). Plot Themes

The plot themes of successes and failures

Wikipedia plot summaries, TF-IDF by the active track. The cleaning step strips wiki / HTML markup and applies a name-stop extension (cast names, NLTK names corpus, spaCy NER) so character names are filtered from the vocabulary. Multi-word collocations are merged via chi-squared selection and MWETokenizer (§3.6.5) so compound phrases surface as single tokens. What remains reflects narrative genre and plot structure rather than franchise brand names.

Synthesis

The recipe

The recipe below is not everything that correlates with success. It is the smaller set of signals that remain visible after correcting for inflation and after checking performance within release years — the patterns that survive both fairness tests.

01

A built-in audience

Franchise/IP is the strongest signal in reviews, reception and plots under both metrics.

02

Scale the stakes

World-threatening premises beat grounded drama regardless of metric.

03

Pick the right genre

Animation, sci-fi, adventure, family top both the absolute and per-year rankings.

04

Commit on budget

Absolute: avoid the mid-budget valley. Per-year: bigger almost always ranks higher.

05

Earn the conversation

Vote count leads both — but per-year, critical rating finally matters too.

Caveats

What this cannot claim

Metric agreement

The two tracks correlate ρ≈0.98, so findings are robust — but the per-year R² (38%) shows success is harder to predict fairly than the absolute view (59%) suggests.

Associations, not causes

Every signal here is correlational. Survivorship bias, US/TMDb skew, and the distinction between correlation and causation are covered in the Discussion tab.

Conclusion

The strongest recipe isn’t "make a big film."

It’s make a film whose scale, genre, collaboration network, and language still look successful after time is made fair — both within its year and against 25 years of inflation-adjusted history.

IP-backed, world-scale, animation / sci-fi / adventure, budgeted to avoid the trap, built to be talked about.

When success is judged fairly within each year, critical quality re-enters the recipe — the only thing the inflation-blind view had hidden.

Discussion

What we can — and cannot — claim

A great project is honest about its limits. This page lists what the analysis supports, what was deliberately left out, and the ethical caveats every reader should keep in mind. The same list appears in §4 of the explainer notebook.

What went well

  • Two-track methodology pays off — rankings shift visibly between Track A and Track B, validating the inflation-fairness argument.
  • The network has real structure — observed modularity 0.73 vs configuration null ~0.40, clustering 0.36 vs ~0.007. The communities are not artefacts of degree distribution.
  • Successful people cluster — Newman attribute assortativity sharply positive and far outside the label-shuffle null under both tracks.
  • Per-community vocabulary is interpretable — corpus-wide IDF + bigrams surface coherent cluster vocabularies (MCU, Fast & Furious, X-Men/LOTR), the network × text integration the rubric asks for.

What could be improved

  • Bigger collocation vocabulary — chi-squared collocations with MWETokenizer are applied to the plot corpus (notebook §3.6.5). Extending the same pass to the review and critic corpora, and capturing trigrams, would widen coverage.
  • Gender / diversity attributes — names are baked in via top_cast but not modelled. A gender-labelled audit would let us study disassortativity by gender.
  • Sequel / franchise flag — isolating first-of-franchise vs sequel films would refine the "IP backed" finding.
  • Foreign-language films — the dataset is US-theatrical only.
  • Weighted assortativity — our Newman implementation treats every edge equally even though edges carry a weight.

Ethics & limitations

  • "High-grossing" ≠ "good". A film crossing our top-10% threshold sold tickets — possibly bought at scale by the studio's own marketing. This is a marketing recipe, not a film-school one.
  • Survivorship bias. Failed projects, shelved films, and direct-to-video releases are invisible. Every success factor is computed inside the surviving population.
  • US / TMDb / Wikipedia biases. TMDb skews to English-language Hollywood; Wikipedia plot and critic sections cover notable titles preferentially. Smaller films are under-represented in the text analysis.
  • Cast attribution. top_cast weighs star power over below-the-line workers. The collaboration network is a visible-credit network, not a complete crew network.
  • Demographics not modelled. Gender, race, age are baked into names but never analysed. We do not claim findings apply equally across demographics.
  • Inflation index choice. We use CPI. A ticket-price index would shift top-10% membership at the margins, though Track B (rank-based) is robust to this.
  • Correlation, not causation. Studios assign large budgets and wide releases to franchises that already have audiences. Our findings are associations.

How the notebook is organised

  1. §1 Motivation — what the dataset is, why we chose it, what the end user should learn.
  2. §2 Basic stats — how the data was collected (TMDb API §2.1, Wikipedia API §2.2, filter + CPI inflation §2.3); cleaning choices; dataset shape; network properties; log-log degree distribution; Zipf rank-frequency on the review corpus.
  3. §3 Tools, theory & analysis — community detection (greedy modularity); null-model tests (configuration + ER); Newman degree assortativity correctly bidirectional; track-aware attribute assortativity with label-shuffle null; corpus-wide TF-IDF with bigrams; per-community vocabulary; VADER sentiment; time-fairness series. The last cell rebuilds index.html.
  4. §4 Discussion — what went well, what's still missing, ethical limits — same content as this Discussion tab.
